subject: Agriculture
title: Insect Farming
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Insect Farming.

hook.text: Black soldier fly larvae convert food waste into protein in 14 days. They eat garbage and become animal feed.

buildup.text: Insect farming requires 1,000 times less land and 500 times less water than beef production per kilogram of protein.

discovery.text: Insect protein is already used in fish feed and pet food. The EU approved mealworms for human consumption in 2021.

twist.text: Two billion people worldwide already eat insects regularly. The Western 'yuck factor' is cultural, not biological.

climax.text: Companies like Protix and InnovaFeed operate factory-scale insect farms producing thousands of tons of protein annually.

punchline.text: Feed waste to bugs, feed bugs to fish, feed fish to humans. Circular protein.

quiz.question: How does insect farming compare to beef in land use?
options: Requires 1,000 times less land per kilogram of protein

details.summary: Insect farming raises species like black soldier flies and crickets for animal feed, human food, and organic waste processing. This topic covers the biology, economics, and environmental advantages of insects as a protein source compared to conventional livestock.
details.whyItMatters: Insects convert feed into protein six times more efficiently than cattle and produce a fraction of the greenhouse gases, offering a scalable alternative as global protein demand rises.
takeaways: Black soldier fly larvae can convert organic waste into high-protein animal feed
Cricket farming uses 2,000 times less water than beef per kilogram of protein
The global insect protein market is projected to exceed $8 billion by 2030

faq.question: Why is insect farming considered sustainable?
faq.answer: Insects reproduce quickly, require minimal land and water, can be raised on organic waste, emit very low greenhouse gases, and convert feed to protein far more efficiently than cattle, pigs, or poultry.

faq.question: What are the main uses of farmed insects?
faq.answer: Farmed insects are used primarily as animal feed (poultry, fish, pets), human food products (protein bars, flour), organic waste processing, and fertilizer production from insect frass, which is nutrient-rich insect excrement.
